claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A pre-edit baseline and an inference procedure that does not supply answer tokens, allowing honest comparison between unedited performance and single-edit results.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 reproduces both required elements: baseline scoring before editing and single-edit evaluation under plain autoregressive decoding. It would establish the same discrepancy, or lack of discrepancy, that this reference experiment addresses.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A semantic evaluation checked against a deterministic token-level measure, so conclusions about editing performance are not dependent on the judgment of one evaluator.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 performs semantic judging across all four dimensions and cross-checks the resulting ranking with match ratio and exact match. It would provide the same instrument-validation evidence.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, normalized measurement of representation change by singular direction, including whether amplification is concentrated in low-variance directions and increases with accumulated edits across methods and architectures.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 specifies the same directional relative-change calculation, SVD-based analysis, low-variance-direction test, edit-count trend, and cross-method/architecture scope. It would directly test the proposed geometric mechanism.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A broad comparative sequential-editing benchmark that tests degradation with edit count, spans major classes of editing approaches and model families, evaluates multiple knowledge benchmarks, and includes a parameter-free comparator.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 matches this scope: eleven methods from the relevant approach classes, four model families, two editing benchmarks, multiple sequential edit counts, all four evaluation dimensions, and a parameter-free retrieval baseline. It would establish the same comparative claim about accumulated degradation and the alternative approach.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct post-edit evaluation of untargeted mathematical and general capabilities at multiple accumulation levels, distinguishing harm to core capabilities from mere failure to edit the target facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 4 evaluates the edited models on the specified untargeted capability suites after 10 and 100 sequential edits. It would reveal whether editing damages capabilities beyond the editing benchmark, which is the discriminating property of this reference experiment.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Stress tests that examine whether the observed limitation generalizes across model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, hyperparameters, and architecture rather than arising from one configuration or fact format.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 5 includes larger models, event-level knowledge, confidence-based fact splits, and AlphaEdit hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity, including execution failures. It would provide the same scope and boundary tests for generality.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set is substantively identical to the six reference experiments. Taken together, it establishes the honest measurement baseline, validates the scoring, tests the geometric mechanism, measures comparative accumulated-editing performance, measures untargeted capability damage, and probes generality across scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and configuration. No reference experiment is left with an evidential gap.
